_README: Answer-key review against Microsoft Learn. Keys are '<section>/<number>' using the source's own numbering. See review.py for the status and confidence vocabulary. Anything absent from this file is NOT_REVIEWED and keeps the dump's key untouched.

std/20.explanation: Tenant restrictions are what stop a user signing in to any tenant other than your own, and in Global Secure Access they are delivered as Universal Tenant Restrictions on the Microsoft traffic profile — that is Microsoft Entra Internet Access. The Global Secure Access feature comparison table lists Universal Tenant Restrictions under the Entra P1/P2 Microsoft traffic profile column only; the Private Access column is blank. Remember the split: Internet Access is the secure web gateway for internet, SaaS and Microsoft traffic, so anything about controlling where users authenticate outbound lives there.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Defender for Endpoint is endpoint detection and response. It does not govern which Entra tenant a user may authenticate to.
C. Microsoft Entra Private Access is the ZTNA half of Global Secure Access, for reaching private on-premises apps. It has no tenant-restriction capability.
D. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB. It can govern SaaS session behaviour but does not enforce tenant restrictions at authentication.

source.title: What is Global Secure Access? — feature comparison table

std/54.explanation: Dangling DNS detection is a named capability of Microsoft Defender for App Service: it alerts when an App Service site is decommissioned and its custom domain (the CNAME) is left behind, which is exactly the subdomain-takeover risk the question describes. The trap here is matching the word 'DNS' in the question to the product with 'DNS' in its name.
whyWrong: A. Defender for DevOps covers the pipeline and repositories, not published DNS records.
C. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS usage.
D. Defender for DNS watches Azure resources for malicious DNS resolution — command-and-control, data exfiltration by DNS — not the lifecycle of a web app's CNAME record.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for App Service — Dangling DNS detection

std/85.explanation:
THIS ANSWER WAS CORRECTED BY AI

Regulatory standards such as NIST SP 800-53 are turned on as security standards in Defender for Cloud — Regulatory compliance > Manage compliance policies > Security policies, then toggle the standard On. Only then does the subscription get assessed and appear on the regulatory compliance dashboard. The original key, assigning a single built-in policy definition from Azure Policy, is wrong twice over: a regulatory standard is an initiative rather than one definition, and assessing it is driven from Defender for Cloud.
whyWrong: A. A built-in policy definition is a single rule. NIST SP 800-53 is a whole initiative, and assigning one definition would not produce a compliance assessment.
B. Defender for Cloud Apps access policies govern SaaS sessions and have nothing to do with regulatory assessment.
D. Secure score recommendations measure general posture against the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, not compliance with a named regulatory standard.

source.title: Assign regulatory compliance standards in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/203.explanation: Adding the regulatory compliance standard in Defender for Cloud is the first step: the standard has to be assigned to the scope before Defender for Cloud will assess the subscription against it or show anything on the regulatory compliance dashboard. Compare this with Standalone 85, which asks the same thing with 'turn on a security standard' as the wording.
whyWrong: A. Secure score reflects the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark, not NIST SP 800-53.
B. A Sentinel data connector moves alerts into a SIEM; it does not assess compliance.
C. The Azure security baseline audit report is a different artefact and is not how a regulatory standard is assessed.

source.title: Assign regulatory compliance standards in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/217.explanation: Flagged: the key is left as the source has it, but it looks wrong and the documentation does not settle the wording. This is the same NIST SP 800-53 scenario as Standalone 85 and 203, except the option 'add a regulatory compliance standard' is missing from the list. The stem already states the subscription has enhanced security enabled, which means the Defender plans in the keyed answer (D) are on — so it cannot be what you do first. Assigning the built-in initiative from Azure Policy (C) is the only remaining action that produces a NIST assessment, and regulatory standards are implemented as Azure Policy initiatives. Treat C as the more defensible answer and verify before relying on this item.

source.title: Assign regulatory compliance standards in Microsoft Defender for Cloud

std/92.explanation: B2B direct connect is the one feature built for Teams shared channels, and it satisfies every requirement in the stem: users collaborate with their home credentials so no guest object is created in contoso.com, inbound cross-tenant access settings can be scoped to a group in fabrikam.com, and the trust gives single sign-on. Microsoft's own wording: users 'work together using their home credentials and a shared channel in Teams, without having to be added to each other's organizations as guests.'
whyWrong: A. B2B collaboration invites the external user as a guest object in your tenant — the opposite of the stated requirement — and guests cannot participate in shared channels.
B. Connect Sync synchronises on-premises AD DS to Entra ID; it is not a cross-tenant feature.
C. Cross-tenant synchronisation provisions external users as B2B collaboration users in your tenant, so it also creates the accounts the question forbids.

source.title: B2B direct connect overview

std/95.explanation: This is the core Global Secure Access split. Microsoft Entra Private Access is the ZTNA service for private, corporate resources — the on-premises App1 — and replaces VPN with per-app access. Microsoft Entra Internet Access is the identity-aware secure web gateway for internet and SaaS destinations, which is what App2 is. Map 'private/on-premises' to Private Access and 'internet/SaaS' to Internet Access and these questions become mechanical.

source.title: What is Global Secure Access?

std/109.explanation: An on-premises FTP server reached from the internet is a private resource on a non-HTTP protocol, and Private Access provides per-app access for TCP and UDP applications with Conditional Access applied per app — that is what makes it ZTNA rather than a VPN. Application proxy would be the older answer but is limited to web apps; Private Access is described as building on application proxy and extending it to any private resource, port and protocol.
whyWrong: B. Microsoft Entra application proxy publishes web applications over HTTP/HTTPS, so it cannot publish FTP.
C. Internet Access secures outbound traffic to internet and SaaS destinations, not inbound access to your own server.
D. Azure Bastion gives RDP/SSH to Azure virtual machines through the portal; Server1 is on-premises and the protocol is FTP.
E. Application Gateway is a regional layer-7 load balancer for HTTP/HTTPS.

source.title: What is Global Secure Access? — Microsoft Entra Private Access

std/214.explanation: Legacy applications issuing LDAP queries need a directory that speaks LDAP. Microsoft Entra Domain Services (formerly Azure AD DS) provides managed domain services — domain join, Group Policy, LDAP, and Kerberos/NTLM — without you deploying or patching domain controllers, which is also what satisfies 'minimize the administrative effort'. Microsoft names this exact scenario: cloud-only organisations with third-party apps that still require LDAP.
whyWrong: B. Azure AD B2C is a customer identity service for consumer sign-in.
C. Azure AD (Microsoft Entra ID) is not an LDAP directory — it speaks OIDC, OAuth and SAML.
D. Running AD DS yourself on Azure VMs works but means deploying, patching and monitoring domain controllers, which is the administrative effort the question tells you to minimise.

source.title: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services

std/215.explanation:
THIS ANSWER WAS CORRECTED BY AI

This is word-for-word the same scenario as Standalone 214, which the source keys to Azure AD DS — so the source contradicts itself, and the Microsoft Entra ID key here is the wrong half of that contradiction. Microsoft Entra ID does not answer LDAP; it is a modern-protocol identity provider. Microsoft Entra Domain Services is the managed domain that provides LDAP, Kerberos/NTLM, Group Policy and domain join for legacy applications that cannot be modernised.
whyWrong: A. AD DS on your own servers would work but is the maximum administrative effort, which the question rules out.
B. Microsoft Entra ID speaks OIDC, OAuth and SAML. Legacy LDAP binds and reads are not supported against it.
D. Microsoft Entra External ID is for external and customer identities.

source.title: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services

std/280.explanation: An enterprise application that needs LDAP to look up attributes about Entra users needs a managed domain in front of Entra ID. Domain Services synchronises users, groups and credentials one way from Microsoft Entra ID and exposes them over LDAP and Kerberos/NTLM, giving the legacy app what it expects without any domain controllers to run.
whyWrong: A. A Conditional Access trusted location is an access-policy condition and adds no directory protocol.
C. Private Access is network access to private apps; it does not make Entra ID answer LDAP.
D. Pass-through authentication validates passwords against on-premises AD DS during sign-in and is unrelated to LDAP lookups against Entra.

source.title: Overview of Microsoft Entra Domain Services
Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/24.explanation: Defender for Identity is the only one of these that looks inside an on-premises AD DS domain. Its identity security posture assessments evaluate domain configuration and surface the weaknesses attackers exploit, which is exactly “identify configuration issues and administrative vulnerabilities”, and it does so from a lightweight sensor on the domain controllers rather than a project you have to build — that is the “minimize effort” half.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Entra ID Protection scores risk on cloud identities (risky sign-ins, leaked credentials). It does not assess AD DS domain configuration.
B. Defender for Servers protects the operating system as a workload, not the directory it belongs to.
D. Microsoft Sentinel is a SIEM. It could ingest the signal, but you would have to write the detections yourself, which is the opposite of minimizing effort.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/101.explanation: Credential exposure in an AD DS domain is Defender for Identity's posture territory: it identifies risky configurations and exposures, analyses lateral movement paths showing how an attacker would traverse the environment, and surfaces the findings as remediation recommendations through Microsoft Secure Score. That combination — actionable recommendations, no infrastructure to build — is what the two requirements are testing.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB for SaaS activity.
B. Secure Score is where some of these recommendations surface, but it is a score, not the product that assesses the domain.
C. The MAP Toolkit is an inventory and migration-planning tool with no security assessment role.

source.title: Microsoft Defender for Identity overview

std/153.explanation: Privilege escalation against a synced on-premises domain is a core Defender for Identity detection: it monitors “privilege escalation and suspicious role or group membership changes” and domain-dominance behaviour such as DCShadow and Golden Ticket. Note the direction of travel — the domain syncs to Entra ID, but the attack happens on-premises, so a cloud identity product cannot see it.
whyWrong: A. Entra ID Protection evaluates cloud sign-in risk, not on-premises privilege escalation.
C. Defender for Servers protects the server workload.
D. PIM governs how Entra roles are activated. It is a preventive control, not a detection for an attack already underway in AD DS.

source.title: Windows LAPS overview

std/27.explanation: Windows LAPS gives every machine a different, automatically rotated local administrator password. Microsoft lists the first benefit as “protection against pass-the-hash and lateral-traversal attacks”, which is the requirement word for word: if one machine's local admin account is compromised, the credential is useless on every other machine, so the ransomware cannot spread sideways with it.
whyWrong: B. Privileged Access Workstations harden the admin’s own device. They do not change the local administrator password on the 500 user machines.
C. PIM does just-in-time elevation for Entra ID roles, not for local Windows accounts.
D. Entra ID Protection detects risky sign-ins and has no role in local account management.

source.title: Windows LAPS overview

std/36.explanation: The question asks what to put in the local Administrators group of a privileged access device, and the keyed answer does not answer that question — configuring LAPS in an emulation mode sets how a password is stored, not who is a member of the group. It is also the wrong direction: Microsoft deprecated the legacy LAPS product as of Windows 11 23H2, and emulation mode exists only to ease migration from an existing legacy deployment. Under least privilege, only Group2 — the team that manages the devices — belongs in the group. The Group1 user who is assigned the device must not be a local administrator on it: that is the whole point of a privileged access device.
whyWrong: B. Legacy Microsoft LAPS is deprecated, emulation mode is a migration aid, and neither configures group membership — which is what the question asks for.
C. Adding the assigned user to the local Administrators group of their own privileged access device breaks least privilege and defeats the purpose of the device tier.

source.title: Endpoint Privilege Management with Microsoft Intune

std/194.explanation: Endpoint Privilege Management lets standard users run specific approved binaries elevated without ever joining the local Administrators group. The detail the question turns on is the elevation type: EPM normally elevates using an isolated virtual account, but its “Elevate as current user” type “runs the elevated process under the signed-in user's own account” — which is precisely the stated requirement that apps run in the context of each signed-in standard user.
whyWrong: B. Windows LAPS manages the local administrator account’s password. Using it means signing in as that separate account, not running as the signed-in user.
C. Cloud Infrastructure Entitlement Management (Entra Permissions Management) governs cloud resource permissions across clouds, not Windows elevation.
D. PIM elevates Entra ID directory roles, not processes on a device.

source.title: Endpoint Privilege Management with Microsoft Intune

std/289.explanation: Installing an application needs administrative rights, and EPM grants exactly that for exactly that binary — elevation is scoped by rules to specific files, logged per elevation, and leaves the user a standard user the rest of the time. Microsoft frames it as supporting Zero Trust by “enabling least privilege access and minimizing lateral movement risks”, which is the phrase the question is pointing at.
whyWrong: A. LAPS would hand Group1 a working local administrator credential — broad standing privilege, the opposite of Zero Trust.
C. PIM covers Entra roles, not application installation on a device.
D. Entitlement management governs access packages for resources, not local elevation.

source.title: Azure Storage firewall rules and network access

std/140.explanation: A network security group cannot protect a storage account at all. NSGs filter traffic at a subnet or network interface inside a virtual network; a storage account is a PaaS service reached through its own public endpoint, which no NSG sits in front of. The control that does this is the storage account firewall: “Each IP network rule enables traffic from a specific public IP address range”, and Microsoft gives the identical example of allowing a client’s public IP. With the firewall configured, only the 20 application servers’ addresses get through and everything else is denied.
whyWrong: A. Service tags are used inside NSG rules, so this fails for the same reason — NSGs do not govern access to a storage account.
B. A Web Application Firewall inspects HTTP for a web application behind Application Gateway or Front Door.
C. Inbound NSG rules govern traffic entering a subnet or NIC, not a storage account.
E. Azure Firewall filters traffic leaving or crossing your network; it is not in the path of an internet client reaching a storage endpoint.

source.title: Lock your Azure resources - considerations before applying locks

std/151.explanation: The requirement that decides this is “minimize the impact on the legacy applications”. A read-only lock blocks the List Keys operation — Microsoft states plainly that “a read-only lock on a storage account prevents users from listing the account keys”, because listKeys is a POST and locks block the control plane. New applications therefore cannot obtain a key, while legacy applications already holding one keep working, since locks do not touch the data plane.
whyWrong: B. Setting AllowSharedKeyAccess to false rejects every request authorized with an account key — it would break the legacy applications outright. Microsoft explicitly says to migrate clients to Microsoft Entra ID before doing this.
C. AllowBlobPublicAccess governs anonymous public read access, a different problem entirely.
D. Rotating keys automatically does not stop anyone from retrieving the current key, and it breaks apps holding the old one.

source.title: Grant limited access to data with shared access signatures (SAS)

std/254.explanation: The keyed answer confuses encryption with access control. Customer-managed keys change which key encrypts data at rest; they grant nobody access and expire for no one. A shared access signature is the delegated-access mechanism, and Microsoft describes it as giving “granular control over how a client can access your data — what resources the client may access, what permissions they have to those resources, how long the SAS is valid”. Scoped to specific blobs, with an expiry, and without making the container public: that is the question restated.
whyWrong: B. Sharing the connection string hands over the account key, granting full access to everything with no expiry.
C. Private Link makes the account reachable privately from a virtual network. External vendors on the internet cannot use it, and it grants no data permissions.
D. Customer-managed keys control encryption at rest. They neither grant nor time-limit access.

std/119.explanation: Flagged as a defective question rather than a wrong key. The stem asks which **two** solutions to include and says each correct answer is a complete solution, but the source records a single letter. Resource-based RBAC in Microsoft Sentinel is what separates the two teams’ log access, and the Azure Monitor agent is what collects the perimeter servers’ event logs — both are needed, and the near-identical Standalone 122 keys exactly that pair. The likeliest explanation is that this copy lost an option or half its key. Answer it as Azure Monitor agent plus resource-based RBAC, and do not treat the graded result here as meaningful.

std/87.explanation: Flagged: the key looks wrong and the source seems to know it. The question asks what forces an upgrade from Microsoft Entra ID Free to Premium; the key says multifactor authentication, but the source’s own explanation links to the Privileged Identity Management documentation, which points at option B instead. That fits the licensing: some MFA is available on the Free tier through security defaults, whereas PIM has always required Entra ID P2. Treat B as the more defensible answer. The key is left as the source has it pending a licensing page check.

source.title: Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent — feature functionality table

std/103.explanation: The feature this question is built on no longer exists. Adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud were deprecated in August 2024, alongside the Log Analytics agent they depended on — Microsoft's retirement table lists the feature with no replacement. The key is left as the source has it because it was right when written, but do not carry this into the exam as a live product: application allowlisting on Windows servers today is App Control for Business, surfaced through Microsoft Defender for Endpoint. The behaviour the stem describes — an allowlist, automatic blocking of anything not on it, and admin approval to promote an app — is what adaptive application controls used to do.

source.title: Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent — feature functionality table

std/283.explanation: Same retired feature as Standalone 103, and the two are the same question with different option lists. Adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud were deprecated in August 2024 with no replacement in that product. The key stands as the source recorded it, but the current answer to this scenario is application control in Microsoft Defender for Endpoint — which is exactly what Standalone 275 keys, and why those two apparently contradictory items are both defensible on their own option lists.

source.title: Prepare for retirement of the Log Analytics agent — feature functionality table

std/275.explanation: Application control policies in Defender for Endpoint (App Control for Business, formerly WDAC) enforce an allowlist on the machine: anything not explicitly allowed is blocked until an administrator authorizes it. Note the contrast with Standalone 103 and 283, which key adaptive application controls in Defender for Cloud — the historically expected answer for this exact scenario, but deprecated in August 2024. Defender for Endpoint's application control is the surviving mechanism, and it is the only option here that controls what executes on a server.
whyWrong: A. Conditional Access App Control proxies SaaS sessions through Defender for Cloud Apps. It governs web sessions, not processes on a virtual machine.
B. OAuth app policies govern third-party apps consented into your tenant, not executables on a server.
C. Intune app protection policies protect corporate data inside mobile apps. They do not allowlist software on Windows Server.

std/60.explanation: Flagged: the key looks wrong but the documentation that would settle it has been retired. The requirement is to plant fake cached credentials on client computers. That is the deception capability, whose lures are fake content — documents, configuration files, cached credentials — planted on specific devices, and which is delivered through Defender for Endpoint (option B). A Defender for Identity honeytoken tag does something different: it marks an existing account as a decoy so any authentication to it alerts, and it plants nothing on any endpoint. That distinction is what Standalone 143 tests correctly. Microsoft's deception articles now redirect to the attack-disruption page, so no citable source establishes it and the source's key is left alone.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/32.explanation: Watermarks are a content marking, and content markings are a sensitivity label setting in Microsoft Purview Information Protection: a label can “mark the content … by adding watermarks, headers, or footers”. Note the scope detail worth remembering — watermarks apply to documents, not to the body of an email, which is why the question asks about attachments.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Cloud Apps is a CASB. It can apply labels to files in third-party services, but it is not what defines the watermark.
B. Insider risk management scores risky user behaviour; it marks nothing.
D. Azure Purview (now the Microsoft Purview Data Map) discovers and catalogues data estates. Content marking belongs to Information Protection.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/124.explanation: The phrase that decides this is “regardless of where the data is stored”. Microsoft describes sensitivity labels as protecting content “wherever it's stored”, because the label is written into the file's metadata and the encryption travels with it — across Windows, macOS, iOS and Android, which matches the mixed device estate in the stem. Classification plus encryption in one control is Information Protection.
whyWrong: A. eDiscovery finds and preserves content for legal matters; it neither classifies nor encrypts.
B. Retention policies decide how long content is kept, not who can open it.
C. Compliance Manager scores your posture against regulations. It is an assessment tool, not a protection control.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/235.explanation: These two work as a pair, which is why the question asks for two components. Sensitivity labels classify the PII and carry the protection with the file; DLP policies act on that classification to stop it leaving — blocking the share, the upload, or the send. Labels decide what something is; DLP decides what may happen to it.
whyWrong: C. Retention labels govern how long content is kept and what happens at the end of its life, not whether it can be shared.
D. eDiscovery cases search and preserve content for investigations and legal hold. They prevent nothing.

source.title: Learn about sensitivity labels

std/88.explanation: Flagged as genuinely contestable rather than wrong. The source keys sensitivity label policies, and that defends well: a label applies encryption whose usage rights follow the file, so an external recipient cannot open it wherever it ends up. But DLP policies are the control literally designed to prevent sharing outside the organisation, and the near-identical Standalone 235 keys the two together as a pair. Either is defensible as written. On the exam, read for the verb: “classify and protect” points at labels, “prevent from being shared” points at DLP, and where both appear the intended answer is usually both.

source.title: Azure Policy definitions effect basics

std/107.explanation: Flagged, because the effect that actually answers this question is not on the list. To evaluate compliance without changing resources you use the **audit** effect, which reports a resource as non-compliant and does nothing else. The keyed answer, **disabled**, does something different: Microsoft's evaluation order says “disabled is checked first to determine whether the policy rule should be evaluated” — it switches the rule off, so nothing is assessed at all. The likely source of the confusion is that a policy *assignment* also has an enforcement mode whose portal label is **Disabled** (DoNotEnforce), and that one does exactly what the question asks: the policy is evaluated and compliance reported, but the effect is not enforced. Two different settings, one shared word. On the exam, keep effect `disabled` (stop evaluating) apart from enforcement mode `Disabled` (evaluate, don't enforce), and remember `audit` is the effect for reporting without changing anything.
whyWrong: A. Deny blocks the request outright, so it very much changes what happens.
C. Modify alters resource properties, for example adding or changing tags.
D. Append adds fields to a resource during creation, so it also changes resources.

source.title: Configure multi-user authorization using Resource Guard

std/69.explanation: This is the rogue-admin scenario, and multi-user authorization with a Resource Guard is the control built for it. The Resource Guard sits in a different subscription or tenant, and Microsoft requires that the backup admin have no Contributor or Backup MUA Operator rights on it — so a compromised backup admin cannot approve their own destructive action. Deleting backups, disabling soft delete and removing MUA protection are all protected operations, and the last two cannot even be exempted.
whyWrong: A. A security PIN gates critical operations for MARS and MABS agents. It is the on-premises analogue, not the control for a Recovery Services vault in this scenario.
C. Registering MABS with a vault is a setup step; it protects nothing by itself.
D. A PIM role assignment for Backup Contributor grants the destructive permission rather than requiring a second party to approve its use.

source.title: FAQ — Protect backups from ransomware with Azure Backup

std/233.explanation: The question asks which controls ensure you can still restore after an attack, and Microsoft answers it directly under “How to block intentional or unintentional deletion of backup data?” — enable soft delete, and require authorization for critical operations. Soft delete is the one that guarantees restorability: it retains deleted backup data for 14 days, and Microsoft warns that “if backups are deleted and soft delete isn't enabled, you or Microsoft can't recover the deleted backup data.” Requiring a PIN for critical operations is the authorization gate offered here. Azure Monitor notifications are a genuine best practice, but they are detective — being told that backups were disabled does not let you restore from them.
whyWrong: A. Alerting on configuration change tells you an attack happened. It does not preserve a recovery point.
C. Offline copies to Data Box is not an Azure Backup control and is not part of Microsoft’s guidance here.
D. Customer-managed keys change who controls the encryption key. They do nothing to stop a backup being deleted.

source.title: FAQ — Protect backups from ransomware with Azure Backup

std/195.explanation: For workloads protected by the MARS agent or Azure Backup Server, the security PIN is the authorization gate on critical operations — disabling backup, deleting backup data, changing a passphrase — so a compromised administrator on the server cannot quietly stop protection before encrypting the estate. That is what “increase the resiliency of the backup strategy” means here: keep the recovery points reachable.
whyWrong: A. Geo-redundant storage protects against a regional outage, not against someone deleting the backups.
B. Customer-managed keys change key ownership; they neither prevent deletion nor preserve recovery points.
D. Site Recovery replicates workloads for disaster recovery. Replication faithfully copies encrypted data too, so it is not a ransomware control.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/96.explanation: The product this question keys no longer exists. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management stopped being available for purchase on 1 April 2025 and was retired on 1 November 2025; its documentation is archived. The key was right when written — Permissions Management was the CIEM tool giving “cross-cloud permissions discovery… for AWS, Azure, and GCP” — so it stands, but do not carry it to the exam as a live answer. Multicloud permission visibility now comes through Defender for Cloud's CIEM capabilities in Defender CSPM.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/262.explanation: Same retired product as Standalone 96. Permissions Management was the tool that measured the gap between permissions granted and permissions used, and could automatically delete permissions unused for the past 90 days — which is why the key matched the stem so exactly. It was retired on 1 November 2025 and its documentation is archived, so treat the underlying idea (find unused entitlements, right-size them) as the examinable point rather than the product name.

source.title: What's Microsoft Entra Permissions Management? (archived — retired 1 November 2025)

std/288.explanation: Access reviews in Privileged Identity Management are the surviving answer. PIM covers Azure resource roles as well as directory roles, so it can enumerate who holds privileged assignments across subscriptions and drive a recurring review of whether they still need them. Note the distractor: option A names the Permissions Management analytics dashboard, which would have been a reasonable answer historically but was retired on 1 November 2025 — so on the current exam this pair is no longer a close call.
whyWrong: A. Microsoft Entra Permissions Management was retired on 1 November 2025.
B. Access reviews in ID Governance cover group and application access; privileged role assignments are reviewed through PIM.
D. Defender EASM discovers your internet-facing attack surface. It has nothing to do with role assignments.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/113.explanation: Azure Policy evaluates resources whenever one is created or updated in a scope with an assignment, and again on a compliance cycle every 24 hours — so a newly deployed non-compliant resource is detected automatically. ISO 27001 ships as a built-in initiative, which is a group of policy definitions assigned together. Note the pairing with Standalone 258: same standard, and Azure Policy is the answer to both, because it is the engine that does the evaluating whichever product surfaces the result.
whyWrong: A. Azure Blueprints is deprecated and packaged artefacts for deployment rather than evaluating ongoing compliance.
B. The regulatory compliance dashboard in Defender for Cloud is where results are read. The evaluation underneath it is Azure Policy, and the question asks what to use to enforce.
C. Azure RBAC governs who may act, not whether the resulting resource is compliant.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/258.explanation: The word that decides this is “remediated”. Azure Policy “helps to bring your resources to compliance through bulk remediation for existing resources and automatic remediation for new resources”, using the deployIfNotExists and modify effects with a remediation task. No other option here changes a resource at all.
whyWrong: A. The regulatory compliance dashboard reports compliance; it remediates nothing on its own.
C. Azure Blueprints is deprecated and deploys artefacts rather than remediating drift.
D. Azure RBAC controls permissions, not resource configuration.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/137.explanation: Restricting which regions resources may be created in is the textbook Azure Policy case — Microsoft lists “Ensure your team deploys Azure resources only to allowed regions” as a headline governance action, and ships a built-in **Allowed Locations** definition with a Deny effect “used to enforce your geo-compliance requirements”.
whyWrong: A. Regulatory compliance standards in Defender for Cloud assess against published frameworks; they do not enforce a company-specific region rule.
B. A custom Azure role decides who can create a resource, not where it may live.
D. Management groups are the scope you assign a policy to, not the mechanism that enforces anything.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/242.explanation: Every recommendation in the list — restrict network access, use virtual network rules, require a private link, disallow public access — is a resource configuration, and Azure Policy is the service that evaluates and enforces resource configuration at scale. Each of these has a built-in definition, and assigning them stops the drift returning rather than just reporting it again next week.
whyWrong: A. Storage Analytics is metrics and logging for a storage account.
B. Network Watcher diagnoses network connectivity and traffic.
C. Sentinel is a SIEM: it would alert on the misconfiguration, not prevent it.

source.title: Overview of Azure Policy

std/163.explanation: The Microsoft cloud security benchmark is delivered as an Azure Policy initiative, so keeping deployed App Service apps compliant with it means assigning that initiative and letting Azure Policy evaluate each app as it is created or updated. The distractors are all about the pipeline rather than the deployed resource.
whyWrong: A. DevOps security in Defender for Cloud assesses the repositories and pipelines, not the running App Service.
B. Defender for App Service detects threats against the running app; it does not enforce a benchmark.
C. A branch policy gates code review before merge, well before anything is deployed.

source.title: Enable vulnerability scanning with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management

std/250.explanation: The product in the key is still right; the requirement in the stem is not. Defender for Servers does provide vulnerability assessment, but it no longer uses the Qualys engine — “Defender for Cloud uses Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management to scan your machines”, in agentless and agent-based modes, and the Qualys-based solution has been retired. A question that asks you to pick a product *because it uses Qualys* can no longer be answered as written. Remember the current pairing: Defender for Servers is the plan, Defender Vulnerability Management is the scanner inside it.

source.title: Enable vulnerability scanning with Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management

std/187.explanation: Hardware and firmware assessment is a premium Defender Vulnerability Management capability, not part of the vulnerability scanning included with Defender for Servers Plan 1. Adding the Defender Vulnerability Management add-on is what turns it on for servers already covered by Plan 1 — which is also why upgrading the plan is not the minimal answer.
whyWrong: A. Moving every server to Plan 2 is a far larger change and is not what gates firmware assessment.
C. Azure Update Manager reports and installs operating system updates; drivers and firmware are not its job.
D. The Intune Suite add-on extends endpoint management features, not server vulnerability assessment.

source.title: Protect folders from ransomware with controlled folder access

std/176.explanation: Controlled folder access exists for exactly this: “Ransomware encrypts your files and holds them hostage. CFA counters this threat by allowing only trusted apps to change files in protected folders.” It is an attack surface reduction capability in Defender for Endpoint, delivered by Microsoft Defender Antivirus, and it protects the user profile folders by default.
whyWrong: B. Azure Files is cloud file storage, not a control on the endpoint.
C. Device Guard (now App Control for Business) controls which code may run, a different control from guarding a folder’s contents.
D. Defender for Endpoint is the platform that contains the feature. The question asks which control to use, and CFA is the specific one.
E. BitLocker encrypts the volume at rest. It does not stop a process running on the signed-in device from encrypting files.

source.title: Protect folders from ransomware with controlled folder access

std/130.explanation: “Protected folders” names the controlled folder access element that does the work — Microsoft defines them as “the folders that CFA guards. Untrusted apps can't modify or delete files in these folders.” This is the same question as Standalone 176 with the option worded differently, and the same reasoning picks it out: the specific control beats the platform it lives in.
whyWrong: A. Defender for Endpoint is the platform; the question asks for the control.
B. Device Guard restricts which code can execute.
D. Azure Files is storage, not an endpoint control.
E. BitLocker protects data if the device is lost or stolen; it is transparent to a process running as the signed-in user.
